plan.topic: Stopping GLP-1 medicines linked to higher heart attack, stroke and death risk: 'metabolic whiplash' in 333,000+ US veterans with type 2 diabetes (WashU)
plan.angle: 'What happens to your body when a GLP-1 stops?' Explain why benefits seem to depend on staying on treatment, and that the effect goes beyond weight: blood pressure, cholesterol and inflammation can drift back. Walk through the study: 333,000+ US veterans with type 2 diabetes followed about 3 years; risk up to 22% higher after about 2 years off; about 18% lower risk with continuous use vs about 12% for people who restarted. Before using these numbers, check the paper for the exact outcome, the comparator for each figure, and the analysed sample. Name the limits clearly: observational ('linked to', not 'causes'); VA population, so mostly older men with T2D, and results may not apply to people without diabetes; people stop for reasons (cost, side effects, illness) that can confound the results. Evidence-based levers for anyone planning a change, strongest first: plan it with your prescriber, keep up monitoring of blood pressure, lipids and A1C (mg/dL and mmol/mol where relevant), protein, strength training and activity habits. Link to what trials show about weight regain after stopping (STEP 1 extension), with the correct population. Never say 'don't stop' or give any switching or tapering advice. Include the exact prescriber line.

package.description:
What happens when you stop a GLP-1? In an analysis of 333,000+ US veterans with type 2 diabetes, being off a GLP-1 for about 2 years was linked to up to 22% higher risk of heart attack, stroke or death than staying on it (a relative number). Restarting was linked to getting some, but not all, of the benefit back. It's observational: a link, not proof.

This video is for education only and isn't medical advice. Don't stop, start or change any medicine without your prescriber. It's a prescription medicine. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

Sources:
1. Xie, Al-Aly et al. GLP-1 RA discontinuation and MACE in type 2 diabetes. BMJ Medicine, 2026: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13007077/
2. WashU Medicine news, 2026: https://medicine.washu.edu/news/stopping-glp-1-drugs-can-quickly-erase-cardiovascular-benefits/
3. Sattar et al. GLP-1 RA meta-analysis. Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol, 2021: https://www.thelancet.com/journals/landia/article/PIIS2213-8587(21)00203-5/abstract
4. Wilding et al. STEP 1 trial extension. Diabetes Obes Metab, 2022: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9542252/
5. Rubino et al. STEP 4. JAMA, 2021: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33755728/
6. Aronne et al. SURMOUNT-4. JAMA, 2024: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38078870/

script.working_title: Stopping a GLP-1: What 333,000 Veterans' Records Showed About Heart Risk
script.target_keyword: what happens when you stop GLP-1
script.hook_pattern: Visceral 'you' scenario + open loop (what happened to people who stopped and then restarted, paid off in 'Stay, stop or restart')

scenes.narration: If you take a GLP-1, it's doing more than turning down your appetite. Right now, it's also nudging your blood pressure, your cholesterol and your blood sugar.

visual.stock_query: friendly body with gauges dialing down

scenes.narration: So what happens to all of that when it stops?
Earlier this year, researchers at Washington University in St. Louis and the VA St. Louis published an analysis of VA health records from more than 333,000 US veterans with type 2 diabetes.
scenes.retention_device: Concrete proof point with big number

scenes.narration: In the team's report, people who had been off their GLP-1 for about two years had up to 22% higher risk of heart attack, stroke or death than people who kept taking it.

visual.stock_query: heart icon with rising line chart

scenes.narration: But this is an observational study. That one detail changes how you should read every number in it.
In the next few minutes, you'll see what the medicine is doing while you take it, what trials show when it's taken away, and what this study can and can't tell you.
And stay for the finding that surprised us most: what happened to people who stopped, and then started again. It isn't quite what you'd expect.

visual.stock_query: calendar with pause and play buttons

scenes.retention_device: Open loop planted (pays off in 'Stay, stop or restart')

scenes.narration: First, what is a GLP-1 actually doing in your body?

visual.stock_query: chapter card gut and brain connected

scenes.narration: GLP-1 is a hormone your gut releases after you eat. It helps your pancreas release insulin when blood sugar rises, slows how fast your stomach empties, and signals fullness to your brain.

visual.stock_query: gut sending messages to pancreas and brain

scenes.narration: Your own GLP-1 is broken down within minutes. The medicines mimic it, but they're built to last far longer, so the signal stays on.
In people with type 2 diabetes, that adds up to more than blood sugar control. A 2021 meta-analysis pooled 8 large trials with about 60,000 people.
GLP-1 medicines were linked to about 14% fewer major heart events, like heart attack and stroke, compared with placebo.

visual.stat_label: Relative, major heart events, 8 T2D trials

scenes.narration: That's a relative number: the event rate was about 14% lower, not 14 out of every 100 people spared. Still, it's randomized trial evidence, the strongest kind.

visual.stock_query: scale weighing two groups of people

scenes.narration: Part of that benefit likely comes from weight loss. Researchers think some also comes from lower blood pressure, better blood fats and less inflammation.
scenes.retention_device: Build the pieces that will 'whiplash' later

scenes.narration: Which raises the obvious question. If the medicine is holding all those numbers down, what happens when you take it away?
scenes.retention_device: Question to viewer before section change

scenes.narration: The cleanest answers come from trials that stopped the medicine on purpose.

visual.stock_query: chapter card stop sign on calendar

scenes.narration: In the STEP 1 trial, adults with overweight or obesity, but without diabetes, took weekly semaglutide or placebo for 68 weeks. Then treatment ended, and 327 participants were followed for another year.
The semaglutide group had lost about 17% of their body weight on average. One year after stopping, they'd regained about two-thirds of it.

visual.stat_label: Of lost weight regained within 1 year

scenes.narration: On average, they were still about 5.6% below their starting weight. Not back to square one, but a big step back.

visual.stock_query: person on staircase stepping back down

scenes.narration: Here's what most headlines skip. Blood pressure, blood fats, A1C and the inflammation marker CRP had improved on treatment.
A year after stopping, most of those improvements had drifted back toward where people started.

visual.stock_query: arrows curving back to start line

scenes.narration: Two more trials tested this head-on. In STEP 4, after 20 weeks on semaglutide, people switched to placebo regained about 7% of their body weight over the next 48 weeks.

visual.stock_query: two paths splitting at a fork

scenes.narration: Those who stayed on it lost about 8% more over the same stretch.
SURMOUNT-4, with tirzepatide, showed the same pattern. People switched to placebo regained about 14% over a year, while those who continued lost another 5.5%.
One catch: all three trials enrolled people without diabetes, and none measured heart attacks after stopping. The veterans study looks at both, and that's where it gets interesting.
So what did more than 333,000 veterans' records show?

visual.stock_query: chapter card file cabinet of records

scenes.narration: The researchers used US Department of Veterans Affairs records for more than 333,000 veterans with type 2 diabetes. About 132,000 had started a GLP-1 medicine, and about 201,000 had started an older diabetes pill called a sulfonylurea, used as a comparison group. They were followed for up to three years.

visual.stock_query: two groups of veterans with records

scenes.narration: They compared people who kept taking it, people who stopped, and people who stopped and restarted, with each other and with the comparison group. The outcome they tracked was combined: heart attack, stroke, or death from any cause.

visual.stock_query: three icons grouped in a box

scenes.narration: The headline: people who had been off the medicine for about two years had up to 22% higher risk of that combined outcome than people who stayed on it.

visual.stat_label: Relative risk, ~2 years off vs 3 years continuous use

scenes.narration: And the team reported that the risk grew the longer people stayed off. Shorter gaps were tied to smaller increases.
Now, 22% sounds huge. But it's a relative number. It doesn't mean 22 out of every 100 people had a heart attack, stroke or died.

visual.fact: The event rate was up to ~22% higher

scenes.narration: It means the event rate was up to about a fifth higher than in people who stayed on it. In absolute terms, over three years, staying on a GLP-1 was linked to about 3.8 fewer events per 100 people than the older pill, stopping and restarting to about 2.4 fewer, and stopping for good to less than 1, a gap too small to rule out chance.

items: All vs. older diabetes pill, 3 years

scenes.narration: So why would stopping be linked to more heart trouble? The study's senior author, Dr. Ziyad Al-Aly, calls it metabolic whiplash.
The idea: the medicine helps keep blood pressure, blood fats, blood sugar and inflammation in check. Take it away, and they may rebound together, like a spring you stop pressing.
That fits what the STEP 1 extension showed, though that trial was in people without diabetes. And it's a proposed explanation, not something this study proved.
Now, the finding we promised at the start: people who stopped, and then started again.

visual.stock_query: chapter card pause and play buttons

scenes.retention_device: Payoff of main open loop begins

scenes.narration: Here's how the three groups compared with the veterans who took the older pill instead. Those who stayed on a GLP-1 for all three years had about 18% lower risk.
People who stopped and later restarted had about 12% lower risk. And people who stopped for good? About 4% lower, a difference too small to rule out chance.
scenes.retention_device: Surprise payoff with a twist question

scenes.narration: So restarting was linked to getting some of the benefit back, but not all of it.
scenes.retention_device: Payoff that opens a new question (why?)

scenes.narration: Why? Nobody knows yet. One possibility is that months of higher blood pressure and blood sugar during the break take a toll that restarting doesn't fully undo.
Another possibility is that people who restart are different in ways the records can't see. And that leads to the most important part of this video.
What this study can't tell you.

visual.stock_query: chapter card magnifying glass on caveats

scenes.narration: This is an observational study. It shows that stopping was linked to higher risk. It can't prove that stopping caused it.

visual.myth: Stopping a GLP-1 causes heart attacks
visual.fact: Stopping was linked to higher risk in an observational study
visual.stock_query: two puzzle pieces not quite fitting

scenes.narration: Here's why that matters. People don't stop medicines at random. Cost, supply problems and side effects like nausea are common reasons. And sometimes people stop because they've gotten sick with something else.
Picture someone who stops because they're in and out of the hospital with another illness. Their heart risk may already be climbing. Stopping could be a sign of that, not the cause.

visual.stock_query: person resting in hospital bed calmly

scenes.narration: Studies like this adjust for things like age and other health conditions. But they can only adjust for what's recorded. Anything unmeasured can still tilt the result. The study also used prescription fills as a stand-in for whether people actually took the medicine, which the authors list as a limitation.
Second limit: who was studied. VA patients are mostly older men. In this study, about 92% were men, the average age was 66, and everyone had type 2 diabetes.

visual.stat_label: Average age 66, all with type 2 diabetes

scenes.narration: So these results may not apply to women, younger adults, or people taking a GLP-1 for weight without diabetes. They weren't the group studied.
scenes.retention_device: Direct 'does this apply to you?' question

scenes.narration: Third: this is one study, published in March 2026. It needs to be replicated in other groups before anyone treats these exact numbers as settled.
scenes.on_screen_text: One study, not the last word

scenes.narration: Still, it lines up with the trial pattern: the benefits seem to depend on staying on treatment. That's a reason to plan, not to panic.
scenes.retention_device: Reassuring pivot, sets up next section

scenes.narration: And here's something that might surprise you: stopping is really common.
A 2025 study of US health records followed adults with overweight or obesity who started semaglutide or liraglutide. Within a year, about 46% of those with type 2 diabetes had stopped.

visual.stat_label: With type 2 diabetes, stopped within 1 year

scenes.narration: Among those without diabetes, it was about 65%. Nearly two in three.

visual.stat_label: Without type 2 diabetes, stopped within 1 year

scenes.narration: A sizable share later restarted. So if you've paused before, you're far from alone. Insurance changes, shortages, side effects and cost can all get in the way.
The goal isn't guilt. It's knowing what to watch, so a change in treatment doesn't catch your body off guard. So what actually helps?
scenes.retention_device: Question to viewer before game plan

scenes.narration: Here are the levers with the strongest evidence, strongest first.
Number one: plan any change with your prescriber. Whether it's cost, side effects or reaching a goal, they can talk through options and set up follow-up, so there's no gap that no one is watching.

visual.stock_query: patient and doctor talking at desk

scenes.narration: Number two: keep up monitoring. Diabetes guidelines call for checking A1C more often when treatment has recently changed, at least every three months.

visual.stock_query: calendar with checkmarks every three months

scenes.narration: For many adults with diabetes, a common A1C goal is under 7%, which is about 53 millimoles per mole. Your own goal may differ, so ask.
For blood pressure, the usual target in diabetes guidelines is under 130 over 80. Your LDL cholesterol goal, in milligrams per deciliter or millimoles per liter, depends on your heart risk.

items: LDL: goal depends on heart risk
A1C: at least every 3 months after a change

scenes.narration: Early warning is the whole point. Rising numbers can be treated, but only if someone is looking.

Number three: protein. When you're eating less, enough protein helps protect muscle. A 2025 joint advisory from four US lifestyle-medicine, nutrition and obesity groups highlighted adequate protein, along with strength training, for people on GLP-1 therapy. If you have kidney disease, ask your care team what amount is right for you.

visual.stock_query: plate with eggs beans and fish

scenes.narration: Number four: strength training. US guidelines recommend muscle-strengthening activity on at least 2 days a week, plus at least 150 minutes of moderate activity.

visual.stat_label: Strength days plus weekly moderate activity

scenes.narration: And here's an encouraging clue. In a Danish trial, adults with obesity first lost weight on a low-calorie diet, then took liraglutide, exercise, both, or placebo for a year.

visual.stock_query: four groups of people on bikes and couches

scenes.narration: A year after all treatment ended, the exercise-only group had kept its weight loss, while the liraglutide-only group regained about 6 kilograms more. The group that combined both also did better than liraglutide alone, but that difference was less certain.
scenes.on_screen_text: Exercise group held its loss after stopping

visual.stock_query: person jogging past finish line smiling

scenes.narration: It was a small trial of people without diabetes, so treat it as a promising signal, not proof.
Number five: everyday habits you can keep, like fiber-rich meals and regular movement. They're the part of the plan that never runs out.
Here's the full checklist. Screenshot it for your next appointment.
So, what happens when a GLP-1 stops? In trials of people without diabetes, weight and heart-related markers tended to drift back within a year.

In an analysis of more than 333,000 veterans with type 2 diabetes, stopping a GLP-1 was linked to higher risk of heart attack, stroke or death than staying on it, and restarting was linked to keeping some, but not all, of the benefit.
It's a link, not proof. But the message is consistent: these medicines seem to work while you take them, a lot like medicines for blood pressure or cholesterol.
Common side effects like nausea often ease over time, and your prescriber can help with them. It's a prescription medicine. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.
Next, we're digging into why some people lose less on a GLP-1, and what response patterns research shows. Subscribe to InforMed so you catch it.

factcheck.summary: The science is accurate and well hedged overall. I checked the main veterans study (S1) against the BMJ Medicine paper, published 18 Mar 2026. These all match: 132,551 on a GLP-1 vs 201,136 on a sulfonylurea; 91.65% men; mean age about 66; median 3-year follow-up; the combined outcome of stroke, heart attack or death from any cause; IRR 0.82, 0.88 and 0.96 (CI 0.92–1.01); absolute differences of 3.76, 2.41 and 0.75 per 100 (CI −0.12 to 1.60); and the stepwise rise with longer breaks (1.04 at 6 months, 1.14 at 1 year, 1.22 at 2 years vs staying on). The prescription-fill proxy and residual confounding limits also match. The WashU press release confirms 333,687 veterans, the 22% figure, 18% and 12%, and Al-Aly's 'metabolic whiplash' quote. These also check out: STEP 1 extension (n=327; −17.3%, regained two-thirds, net −5.6%, cardiometabolic markers drifting back toward baseline), Sattar 2021 (8 trials, about 60,000 people, HR 0.86), the Rodriguez 2025 rates (46.5% and 64.8% stopped; 47.3% and 36.3% restarted) and the Jensen 2024 regain (6.0 kg). Relative vs absolute risk, correlation vs causation, the population limits, the kidney-disease caveat for protein and the prescriber line are all handled well. One major fix: s52 describes the drugs in the Rodriguez study wrongly. It included tirzepatide, not only semaglutide and liraglutide. The rest is minor wording and source hygiene.

issues.claim: A 2025 study of US health records followed adults with overweight or obesity who started semaglutide or liraglutide.
issues.problem: The JAMA Network Open study (Rodriguez 2025) followed 125,474 people who started a dual-labeled GLP-1 medicine: liraglutide, semaglutide or tirzepatide. Tirzepatide was in the main group (13–14.5% of people). Naming only two drugs gets the study wrong.
issues.fix: A 2025 study of US health records followed more than 125,000 adults with overweight or obesity who started semaglutide, liraglutide or tirzepatide. Within a year, about 46% of those with type 2 diabetes had stopped.

issues.claim: the liraglutide-only group regained about 6 kilograms more
issues.problem: It doesn't say what the 6 kg is compared with. The paper reports 6.0 kg more regain after liraglutide than after supervised exercise. Without that, viewers could read it as 6 kg more than at the start, or more than placebo.
issues.fix: A year after all treatment ended, the exercise-only group had kept its weight loss, while the liraglutide-only group regained about 6 kilograms more than the exercise group. The group that combined both also regained less than liraglutide alone, but that difference was less certain.

issues.claim: Right now, it's also nudging your blood pressure, your cholesterol and your blood sugar.
issues.problem: This states an effect as certain for every viewer. The evidence shows average improvements in trials, and the effect on cholesterol is modest and varies from person to person.
issues.fix: If you take a GLP-1, it's doing more than turning down your appetite. On average, it also helps nudge down blood pressure, blood fats and blood sugar.

issues.claim: In this study, about 92% were men, the average age was 66
issues.problem: The 91.65% figure is for the GLP-1 group. It's close enough, but the wording should say which group it describes.
issues.fix: In this study, about 92% of GLP-1 users were men, the average age was about 66, and everyone had type 2 diabetes.

issues.claim: Publisher: American Journal of Clinical Nutrition / Obesity
issues.problem: The linked PMC page (PMC12264624) is the Obesity Pillars version of the joint advisory, which was published in several journals. The publisher field doesn't match the URL.
issues.fix: Set the publisher to "Obesity Pillars (co-published in AJCN and Obesity); Mozaffarian D et al."

hold_reason: Dropped by Editor-in-Chief: The main veterans study is reported accurately and hedged well, and the audio, visuals and packaging are all fine. I'm dropping it because the major error in s52 was never fixed: it says the Rodriguez 2025 stop and restart rates come from semaglutide or liraglutide users only, but that study also included tirzepatide. That's the kind of scope error we dropped S1 for. A re-render using the fact-checker's wording, plus the minor fixes to s65 (what the 6 kg is compared with) and the thumbnail ('With T2D'), should clear it.

audio.soundNotes: Music sits at -13.5dB under voice and -14.9dB in pauses, both already inside target; nudged gain to 1.1 to lift pauses closer to -14dB without pushing under-speech level past -12dB. Main fixes: pulled down several cues that measured far too hot during speech (-3.8 to -9.2dB, well above the -14 to -20dB felt target) at t=144.6-145.0, 233.3, 407.8, 497.3, 612.6, 641.8-641.9, 715.6 and 718.9. Thinned three SFX swarms that exceeded the 3-4-per-second guideline: the swoosh pile-up at t=22.2-22.9 (kept tick+swell+one ding+one swoosh), the rapid bubble/swoosh repeats at t=338.7-339.0 (kept opening and one closing hit), the LDL chip-reveal swarm at t=592.4-592.8 (15 overlapping cues cut to 4: opening whoosh, swell accent, closing blip), and the redundant swoosh doubles at t=598.0 and the extra pop/swoosh at t=439.4-439.8. Added five bespoke, story-specific accents for moments the stock kit can't cover: a somber heartbeat under the heart-attack/stroke/death chip, a low tension drone under 'longer off, higher risk', a suspense sting on 'one catch', a paper/records rustle introducing the VA health-records study, and a subtle time-lapse whoosh-reversal on 'metabolic whiplash' - all kept low (0.2-0.35) so they read as texture, not accents that fight the narration.

issues: Arrow direction is slightly ambiguous (could read as injecting rather than stopping) but still an eye-catching device
Headline 'Metabolic Whiplash' is punchy but doesn't tie directly to 'stopping' or 'veterans' cue from the title
No face/expression on the heart lowers emotional pull compared to the other two
Blue-on-blue palette has less contrast/pop in a crowded feed than the purple or red versions
Three-line headline is legible but slightly denser than the others
Qualifier line 'LINKED RISK, ~2 YRS OFF' is very small at phone-feed and small sizes — likely unreadable in under a second
Big number claims a specific stat that must exactly match the veteran-cohort study's reported figure or it risks being misleading
White qualifier pill crowds the bottom-left near the hero art, adding visual clutter at small sizes

thumbnail.reasoning: All three use the same heart-mascot device and brand palette, so the deciding factors are emotional pull, clarity of the curiosity gap, and phone-size legibility. #2 ('UP TO 22%') has the strongest raw curiosity/loss-aversion pull and aligns with the playbook's preference for concrete numbers, but its required qualifier line ('LINKED RISK, ~2 YRS OFF') renders too small to read at phone-feed size, dropping its legibility below the ≥7 bar — and without that qualifier visible, the bare '22%' risks reading as an overstated, unhedged claim, which conflicts with brand accuracy rules. #1 is clean and legible but the plain black question-mark heart lacks a face or strong emotion, giving it the weakest scroll-stopping power of the three. #0 ('Metabolic Whiplash') pairs a highly legible, punchy two-word headline with an expressive, surprised face and a motion arrow that visually reinforces 'something changes when you stop' — strong contrast, single clear focal point, and no readability risk at small sizes. It clears the legibility bar comfortably while still offering strong curiosity, so it's the best pick.

issues.problem: The thumbnail doesn't name the population, which was veterans with type 2 diabetes. The title says it, but a viewer on GLP-1 for weight only could see just the thumbnail and think the result applies to them. The script specifically warns that it may not.
